name: University Corporation for Atmospheric Research

profile.reading:
The NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center is a purpose built high performance computing facility in Cheyenne, Wyoming, operated by NSF NCAR, the National Center for Atmospheric Research, under the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research, a nonprofit consortium of universities that manages NCAR on behalf of the National Science Foundation. The center opened its doors in 2012 following a partnership among UCAR and NCAR, the State of Wyoming, the University of Wyoming, the Cheyenne LEADS economic development organization, the Wyoming Business Council, and the local electric utility, then known as Cheyenne Light, Fuel and Power and now part of Black Hills Energy. Wyoming was chosen as a site in part for its relatively low cost, wind and hydro influenced electricity supply and its cool, dry climate, both favorable to the energy demands and cooling economics of a large scientific computing installation.

The facility exists to house NSF funded supercomputers dedicated to climate, weather, and broader atmospheric and geosciences research rather than commercial or general purpose enterprise computing. Its flagship systems have been replaced in succession as computing needs and technology have advanced. Yellowstone was the original system installed at opening in 2012, followed by a system named Cheyenne, and more recently by Derecho, the current NSF NCAR supercomputer, whose installation NCAR has documented publicly, including through a published time lapse video of the system going into the building. Since opening, NCAR reports that more than 4,000 researchers from more than 575 universities and other institutions have used the center's computing and data storage resources, reflecting its role as shared national scientific infrastructure rather than a facility serving a single institution.

Unlike commercial data centers, NWSC does not publish its capacity in colocation industry terms such as critical IT megawatts or raised floor square footage on its public facing materials, and no such figures were located in the operator's own published overview of the center. What NCAR does publish, and actively promotes, is public access. The site includes a visitor center open to walk in visitors on weekdays, with no admission fee, offering exhibits on weather, climate, supercomputing, and atmospheric research, and docent led tours available to school groups from the ninth grade up through the general public, bookable online. That combination, a mission driven research computing facility built and owned through a public private partnership, largely funded by federal science spending, and deliberately opened to public visitors, distinguishes NWSC from most other entries in a directory otherwise dominated by commercial and hyperscale data centers.

reading:
The University Corporation for Atmospheric Research is a nonprofit consortium of universities based in Boulder, Colorado that manages the National Center for Atmospheric Research for the National Science Foundation. It is in this registry as an academic operator, and the one facility recorded under it is the NCAR Wyoming Supercomputing Center at 8120 Veta Drive in Cheyenne, Laramie County, Wyoming, which opened in 2012 and is staffed by the NSF NCAR Computational and Information Systems Laboratory. UCAR reports that the center has served more than 4,000 users from more than 575 universities and other institutions.

The facility exists because of a specific public partnership rather than a commercial siting decision, and the partners are named on UCAR's own page: UCAR and NCAR, the State of Wyoming, the University of Wyoming, the Cheyenne LEADS economic development organization, the Wyoming Business Council, and the local electric utility then called Cheyenne Light, Fuel and Power and now part of Black Hills Energy.

The most useful technical record is not the operator's marketing but the National Science Foundation environmental assessment prepared for the project in March 2010. It describes a 24 acre site in Cheyenne's North Range Business Park, at the northwest corner of Prosperity Drive and Logistics Drive, and an initial core and shell module of roughly 100,000 gross square feet. Inside that, it lays out two raised floor computer halls of approximately 12,000 square feet each, about 50,000 square feet for mechanical and electrical plant, roughly 10,000 square feet of office and visitor space and about 6,000 square feet for data storage. Each raised floor space was designed to accommodate approximately 6 to 8 megawatts of total electrical load, and the design target for power usage effectiveness was below 1.3. Power was to come from the Happy Jack substation over a high voltage transmission line, with Cheyenne Light, Fuel and Power as the serving utility.

That 6 to 8 megawatts per hall is a design figure from a pre construction federal filing, describing total electrical load the space was built to take. It is not a published operating IT load, and neither UCAR nor NSF publishes what the building actually draws today. The center's capacity is normally described instead in terms of the machines it houses, which have run in succession as Yellowstone, then Cheyenne, and now Derecho. This registry therefore records no critical IT megawatt figure for the site and treats the environmental assessment numbers as design intent.
